claims.text: A core–shell microstructure enables lightweight high-entropy alloys to combine low density, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance.
Spatial segregation of structural and protective functions permits simultaneous optimization of density, strength, and environmental durability.
Annealing a uniform HEA at 700°C for 1–4 hours under an inert atmosphere will induce surface segregation and form a core–shell structure.
The intended structural mediator is a passivating surface shell over a low-density, mechanically robust core.
The heat treatment causes corrosion-resistant elements to migrate toward the alloy surface.
Cr, Mo, or Ni can constitute the corrosion- and oxidation-resistant surface enrichment.
The interior remains enriched in lightweight and strength-promoting elements such as Al, Ti, and V.
The enriched shell protects the alloy from aggressive environmental species.
Confining lightweight and strength-promoting elements primarily to the core preserves low density and mechanical strength.
Excessively long or severe annealing dissipates the compositional gradient through homogenization.
Loss of the compositional gradient eliminates the protective mechanism.
Relative to an untreated uniform HEA, the core–shell-treated alloy will have significantly better corrosion resistance.
Relative to an untreated uniform HEA, the core–shell-treated alloy will have significantly better high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Formation of the core–shell structure will cause little or no loss of requisite mechanical strength.
Formation of the core–shell structure will cause little or no compromise in low density.
Homogenization during over-extended annealing will remove the shell and negate the performance advantages.
The controlled comparison uses an otherwise comparable uniform HEA without post-synthesis segregation heat treatment as the baseline.
The hypothesis predicts a correlation between loss of the core–shell structure during extended annealing and degradation of corrosion or oxidation performance.
